contents.text: The way an amino acid chain folds into a protein depends on the chemical properties of its amino acids. If one amino acid is replaced by another with different chemical properties, the protein's folding, shape, and function may be drastically affected, ultimately impacting the organism's phenotype.
Read the passage about hemoglobin proteins.

textContent.text: Normal hemoglobin proteins hold oxygen in red blood cells to be distributed throughout the body.

In a hemoglobin translated from a mutated gene, glutamic acid, a hydrophilic (water-loving) amino acid, is replaced by valine, a hydrophobic (water-fearing) amino acid. Unlike glutamic acid, valine sticks to hydrophobic amino acids in other hemoglobin proteins, forming protein chains. These stiff chains bind oxygen poorly and cause the red blood cell to take a sickled shape. This condition, called sickle cell disease, causes blood cells to get stuck in small blood vessels and can cause pain, fatigue, and other symptoms.
